solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Open fabric marker kept in series for amateur handicraft

indicators.note: something kept in another thing sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: scrim is a loosely woven open cloth used in theatres and upholstery
ser. is the standard abbreviation for series
a hand is the pointer that marks the time on a clock

explanation.surface: A craft instruction: open-weave fabric with a marker pen held inside, part of a series of amateur projects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marker' suggests a pen, but it is the pointer on a clock face; ser. is a standard abbreviation solvers may not know.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives scrimshander as a form of scrimshaw, the carving on bone or shell done by sailors as a pastime.

clue.text: Robots, say, at work ousting heart of plant? It may evince sympathy (8, two words)

indicators.note: ousting throws something out, so the named letter is removed from the fodder
letters at work are busy being moved about, so they are rearranged
'heart of' keeps only the middle letter of 'plant'

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the middle letter of the five-letter word plant

explanation.surface: Robots at work replacing a factory's core staff, a tale meant to win our sympathy.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the A of plant from ROBOTS SAY, then rearrange what is left. 'Plant' reads as a factory, but only its middle letter matters.
explanation.definitionFit: A sob story is a tale of hardship told to arouse pity, which is exactly what evincing sympathy means here.

clue.text: A very long day in tropical parts

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the following words, running across them

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A long day spent somewhere in the tropics.
explanation.walkthrough: Calpa (or kalpa) is a Hindu cosmic term, which is why 'very long' is an understatement.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hindu cosmology a calpa is a day of Brahma, lasting over four billion years, so a very long day indeed.

clue.text: Occasion, we hear, for a poet's tears

indicators.note: we hear points to a word that is listened to, so its sound is what counts, not its spelling

blocks.note: room means occasion or opportunity, as in no room for doubt

explanation.surface: An event that moves a poet to weep.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheum is watery discharge from the eyes; poets used it for tears, as Shakespeare does.

clue.text: Mark, one seen on note becoming due

blocks.note: M is an abbreviation for mark, the old German currency
a means one
Alan Turing appears on the Bank of England fifty-pound note issued in 2021

explanation.surface: Someone spots a mark on a banknote as a bill falls due.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' suggests music, but here it is a banknote: Alan Turing became the face of the new British fifty-pound note in 2021.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill or policy is maturing when it reaches the date on which payment must be made.

clue.text: Site with a smash littered round roundabout? It stops circulation

indicators.note: littered things are scattered untidily, so these letters are strewn into a new order
round places the scrambled letters on either side of the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
a roundabout is circular, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: A traffic scene: crash debris strewn around a roundabout, bringing circulation to a halt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circulation' looks like traffic flow but means the blood, and a roundabout is just an O.
explanation.definitionFit: Haemostasis is the medical stopping of bleeding, halting the flow of blood through or out of a vessel.

clue.text: Score a couple of centuries, lifting hearts

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting raises the letters so they read from bottom to top

blocks.note: C is the Roman hundred and a ton is a century in cricket, two hundreds side by side
H is the card abbreviation for hearts

explanation.surface: A batsman scores two hundreds and lifts the spirits of the fans.
explanation.walkthrough: A ton is a hundred runs in cricket; the two centuries are turned upwards before hearts is added.
explanation.definitionFit: To score is to cut a notch, the old way of keeping a tally, so the noun or verb matches.

clue.text: Awfully dour over clothes getting soaked in the Trossachs?

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, so the letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
kit means a set of clothes, as in sports kit

explanation.surface: A grim walker's clothes get soaked on a wet day in the Scottish hills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' sets the scrambled word above KIT in this down entry. The Trossachs are a Scottish Highland area, which flags a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Droukit is the Scots past participle of drouk, to drench, so it means soaked through.

clue.text: Valence adjusted for restricted area

indicators.note: adjusted letters have been altered and moved around into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A chemistry note: a valency changed to suit a restricted zone.
explanation.definitionFit: An enclave is a territory enclosed within another, a separate bounded area.

clue.text: Light rain effective action cleared from street

indicators.note: cleared from says one thing is taken away from another, leaving a remainder

blocks.note: a stroke is a telling move, as in a stroke of genius
St is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Drizzle makes it pointless to take action to clear the street.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove ST from the front of STROKE.
explanation.definitionFit: Roke is a dialect word for mist, smoke or fine drizzle, hence light rain.

clue.text: Trouble getting in fish for tourist hotel

indicators.note: getting in means entering, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a parr is a young salmon
ado is fuss or bother

explanation.surface: A fishing holiday goes wrong at the hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: A parr is a young salmon; paradors are Spanish, so the fish and the trouble give no hint of Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: A parador is a Spanish state-run hotel, often in a historic building, aimed at tourists.

clue.text: Upright, active, this lot work making a point (11, three words)

blocks.note: roman type is upright, as opposed to italic
a is the grammar abbreviation for active
these refers to this group of things

explanation.surface: A grammar or printing rule: upright, active words for this group make the point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upright' sounds moral but is the typeface; roman type stands straight, unlike italic.
explanation.definitionFit: A roman à thèse is a novel written to argue a thesis, a work of fiction with a point to prove.

clue.text: Liberal taken in by trend, once deluded

indicators.note: taken in by means held inside, so the first piece is enclosed by the second

blocks.note: a bent is an inclination or tendency
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A politician fooled by fashion, in the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: L sits inside BENT; 'once' marks the word as archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Blent is an old past tense of blend in its obsolete sense of blind or delude, so it means misled.

clue.text: Handle sword-thrust as of old

blocks.note: first meaning: the handle or butt of a gun or tool
second meaning: an archaic word for a thrust in fencing

explanation.surface: A fencing lesson on dealing with an old-fashioned thrust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handle' reads as a verb, cope with, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A stock is the wooden part held in the hand, and Shakespeare uses stock for a straight thrust, from stoccado.

clue.text: Hawking may produce this subject in result

indicators.note: in places the first piece within the second

blocks.note: a sum is the result of adding
to subject someone to something is to put them to it

explanation.surface: Stephen Hawking producing a subject that yields a result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hawking' suggests the physicist, but here it is clearing the throat noisily.
explanation.definitionFit: To hawk is to cough up phlegm, and sputum is the spittle and mucus brought up.

clue.text: Spot roughly treated mostly round front of chin

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
round places the shortened word around the next letter
'front of' keeps only the first letter of 'chin'

blocks.note: mauled means handled roughly
the first letter of chin

explanation.surface: A blemish on a face that has been roughed up, near the chin.
explanation.walkthrough: MAULED loses its D, then wraps around C.
explanation.definitionFit: A macule is a small flat spot or blemish on the skin, the medical word for a mark.

clue.text: Wild buffalo? I appreciate that wafted aroma

indicators.note: something wafted drifts about in the air, so the letters are blown into a new order

blocks.note: ta is an informal British thank-you
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone thanks another for the smell of a wild buffalo carried on the breeze.
explanation.definitionFit: The tamarao is a small wild buffalo native to the Philippine island of Mindoro.

clue.text: Salvoes creating fury in drinking places

indicators.note: in sets the first piece inside the second

blocks.note: bars are places to drink
rage is fury

explanation.surface: A pub brawl where volleys of abuse spread rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creating' is only a link here, joining the definition to the wordplay that builds it.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrage is a heavy burst of artillery fire, so barrages are repeated salvoes.

clue.text: Old pavilions? Matches will include one

indicators.note: to include something is to take it within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a copy matches its original
an is the indefinite article, meaning one

explanation.surface: Cricket talk: old pavilions where matches will include a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pavilions' and 'Matches' suggest cricket, but matches is a verb meaning duplicates.
explanation.definitionFit: Canopy once meant a tent or pavilion; Chambers marks this sense as obsolete, hence old.

clue.text: Miss spread out in bedroom I tickled

indicators.note: spread out in says the letters stretch across several words of the clue

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word through the second into the third

explanation.surface: A playful bedroom scene with a young woman tickled on the bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a young woman but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To miss something out is to leave it out, which is to omit it.

clue.text: Set out in deep thought for tourist priority?

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are knocked out of place and rearranged
in places the rearranged letters inside the following word

blocks.note: to muse is to think deeply; here the noun
taken as written

explanation.surface: A traveller lays out plans after deep thought about what to see first.
explanation.definitionFit: A must-see is an attraction regarded as essential viewing, the sight a visitor puts first.

clue.text: Top lady exchanges lid for one to have a favourable effect

indicators.note: exchanges means swapping one thing out for another

blocks.note: an empress is a woman at the very top of an empire
the lid is the top letter, here of the word just given
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A queen swaps her hat for another to make a good impression.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letter of EMPRESS, its lid, is replaced by I.
explanation.definitionFit: To impress is to make people think well of you, producing a good effect on them.

clue.text: Salt sprinkled via aid to digestion

indicators.note: sprinkled things are scattered about, so the letters land in a new order

blocks.note: sal is the Latin and chemistry word for salt
taken as written

explanation.surface: Salt is sprinkled on food to help the digestion along.
explanation.definitionFit: Saliva contains enzymes that begin breaking down starch, so it starts the digestive process.

clue.text: Stomachs financial undoing, one involving millions

indicators.note: involving means wrapping something up within, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: ruin is financial collapse
M stands for million
a means one

explanation.surface: Someone's stomach churns at losing millions in a financial crash.
explanation.walkthrough: M goes into RUIN, and A follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Rumina is the plural of rumen, the first stomach of a cud-chewing animal.

clue.text: Jock's stabbing pain catches back

indicators.note: back says the word is read in the reverse direction

blocks.note: to net is to catch

explanation.surface: A Scot gets a sharp pain while catching, perhaps in cricket, and hurts his back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like part of the body with the pain, but it only turns the word round. Jock is a nickname for a Scot, flagging a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sten is Scots for a sudden sharp stitch or stabbing pain.

clue.text: Military supremo at head of troops, rarely surrounded

indicators.note: 'head of' keeps only the first letter of 'troops'

blocks.note: C-in-C, Commander-in-Chief
the first letter of troops

explanation.surface: A commander leading troops, seldom caught surrounded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rarely' belongs to the definition, marking a rare word.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinct is a rare word meaning girdled or encircled, from Latin cinctus.

clue.text: Ice cream confection in pastry – something out of this world

blocks.note: a tart is a pastry case with filling
an unidentified flying object, supposedly from another world

explanation.surface: A dessert in pastry that tastes out of this world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of this world' sounds like praise for the dessert but is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A tartufo is an Italian dessert, a ball of ice cream coated in cocoa or chocolate to look like a truffle.

clue.text: Salt cellar initially passed for junior cleric at bishop's tea party

indicators.note: passed means skipped over, so that letter is left out
'initially' keeps only the first letter of 'cellar'

blocks.note: the first letter of cellar

blocks.clueFragment: junior cleric at bishop's tea party
blocks.note: the famous Punch cartoon of the curate's egg, served at the bishop's breakfast table

explanation.surface: At a bishop's tea a salt cellar is passed to a nervous young clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the C from CURATE. The curate's egg, 'good in parts', comes from an 1895 Punch cartoon of a curate dining with his bishop.
explanation.definitionFit: A urate is a salt of uric acid, as found in gout deposits.

clue.text: Commotion with withdrawal of US has me mostly gripped in worries

indicators.note: withdrawal means pulling out, so the named letters are removed
mostly means not quite all, so a final letter goes
gripped in means held inside, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: fuss is commotion
taken as written
me is the setter, Azed

explanation.surface: An American pulling out causes fuss, and the setter is gripped by worry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Me' in an Azed clue is the setter himself, so his pseudonym, cut short, supplies the middle letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To faze is to disconcert or perturb, so fazes means worries as a verb.

clue.text: Old bird, one hiding its head, but not that one!

indicators.note: hiding its head means the first letter is concealed, so it is dropped

blocks.note: the bird proverbially said to bury its head in the sand

explanation.surface: An old bird that hides its head in the sand, but it is not the ostrich.
explanation.walkthrough: Behead OSTRICH. 'But not that one' warns that the beheaded bird is a different bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Strich is an obsolete word for the screech owl, a bird of old usage.

clue.text: One submitting petition, good but with page missing

indicators.note: missing means absent, so that letter is left out

blocks.note: super means very good
p is the abbreviation for page

explanation.surface: A petitioner is good but has lost a page of the document.
explanation.walkthrough: Take P out of SUPER.
explanation.definitionFit: A suer is someone who sues, either at law or in the older sense of pleading or entreating.

clue.text: Autocrat, one in pieces suffering setback

indicators.note: in places the first piece inside the second
a setback sends things the other way, so the combined letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: parts are pieces
a means one

explanation.surface: A despot whose regime falls apart after a reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: A goes inside PARTS, between T and S, and the whole is then turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A satrap was a provincial governor in ancient Persia, and by extension any petty tyrant or despot.

clue.text: University enraptured was unwonted

blocks.note: U is the abbreviation for university
sent means thrilled or carried away

explanation.surface: A student finds university unexpectedly thrilling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unwonted' looks like unusual, but here it is an old verb, not to be accustomed.
explanation.definitionFit: Usent is an obsolete form meaning was not accustomed, the past of an old verb for being unused to something.

clue.text: Veteran fighter Ben's driven from Libyan city

indicators.note: driven from means expelled, so those letters are pushed out of the word

blocks.note: taken as written
Benghazi is Libya's second city

explanation.surface: An old soldier called Ben is expelled from a Libyan city.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove BEN from the start of BENGHAZI.
explanation.definitionFit: A ghazi is a Muslim warrior, especially one who has fought against non-believers, and a title given to veterans.

clue.text: Scrap metal? Science taking lead, without turning back

indicators.note: turning back means facing the other way, so that word is read in reverse

blocks.note: sci. is the abbreviation for science
less means without, as in a year less a day

explanation.surface: A query about whether science leads the way in recycling scrap metal, without going back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking lead' only says SCI comes first; 'lead' is not the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Scissel is the metal clippings left over after coins or blanks are punched from a sheet.

clue.text: Sign of a bad night? Remains on edge, left with shattered senses

indicators.note: shattered means broken into bits, so the letters are reassembled in a new order
on edge places a word on both edges of the other letters, around them

blocks.note: rests are what remains, the remainders
L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tired and edgy after a sleepless night, their senses frayed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On edge' looks like nervousness, but it is the instruction to put one word around the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Restlessness is an inability to settle or sleep, the typical result of a disturbed night.
